text: {"lesson":{"schemaVersion":1,"title":"Lesson 2: Ancient Greece in Words Only","lessonType":"spark","header":{"focusStandards":["L.6.4.a","RI.6.1","RI.6.7","RI.6.9"],"supportingStandards":["SL.6.1"],"eldStandards":["ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PII.6.3"],"mediaLiteracyStandards":[],"objectives":[{"kind":"content","text":"Students will read short excerpts from three informational texts, extract 3-4 facts about ancient Greek life, beliefs, learning, or daily challenges, and use them to predict what kinds of fears, natural events, and mysteries Greek myths would explain."},{"kind":"content","text":"Students will compare their predictions with those of groups who read different texts, and explain how the authors present ancient Greece differently, to understand how myths arise from cultural needs."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will use context clues to determine the meaning of key words, and will use present-tense reporting verbs and modal verbs (e.g., the text states..., this suggests..., stories might explain...) to share evidence and predictions."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will practice fluency (accuracy and prosody) by reading a short excerpt aloud, pausing to reflect meaning and tone, and then explaining why the author paused and what idea is emphasized."}],"essentialQuestions":["Why do people create stories to explain the world?","How do the beliefs and challenges of a culture shape the stories it tells?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"In Lesson 1, students explored why cultures create myths and inferred the problems in unlabeled Prometheus and Pandora passages. Today they build the cultural and historical context of ancient Greece through words alone, with no images.","enduringUnderstanding":"Myths are not just entertaining stories; they grow out of what a culture fears, needs, and wants to understand.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 3, students will hear how Rick Riordan thinks about what myths do for people and how he adapts them. Today's predictions about Greek fears and mysteries will help them judge his ideas, and later read The Lightning Thief with this context.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students will analyze the cultural values behind myths and compare sources. Today they practice pulling facts from several texts and comparing how different authors present the same world."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"context clue","definition":"a word, phrase, or sentence near an unfamiliar word that helps a reader figure out its meaning","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"phenomenon","definition":"an event or fact in nature that can be observed, such as a storm or an eclipse","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"myth","definition":"a traditional story, often about gods or heroes, that explains something about the world or a culture's beliefs","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"prediction","definition":"a thoughtful guess about what will happen or what something will be like, based on evidence","tier":"support"},{"word":"prosody","definition":"the rhythm, pausing, and expression of reading aloud that shows meaning and tone","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"A Short History of Greek and Roman Myth","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs (about 3-5 sentences)"},{"title":"Ancient Greece: The First Greeks","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs (about 3-5 sentences)"},{"title":"Ancient Greek Thinkers, Truth Seekers","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs (about 3-5 sentences)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they learned about why cultures create myths, practice the unfamiliar word phenomenon using context, and preview the day's task of learning about ancient Greece from words alone.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Why Would Stories Come From a World Like This?","minutes":15,"standards":["L.6.4.a","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use the Turn and Talk routine to discuss: Think back to Lesson 1. What kinds of things did people in the past use stories to explain?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you learn yesterday about why cultures create stories about gods, nature, and the unknown?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"People made stories to explain things they couldn't understand, like storms or why bad things happen. In the Prometheus and Pandora passages, the stories explained where fire and troubles came from."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we will learn about the real world of ancient Greece, but there is a challenge. You will have no pictures, only words. You will become detectives who find facts in the text and use them to predict what Greek stories might explain."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Display this sentence: *Ancient Greeks watched a strange phenomenon, a sudden thunderstorm, and believed that Zeus was angry.* (Teacher-written sentence for modeling.)"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's use a context clue to figure out the word *phenomenon*. Look at what is near it. The sentence names a thunderstorm right after the word and says it made people think of an angry god. So a phenomenon must be an event in nature that people can observe. Context means the words around a word can hold its meaning."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words near *phenomenon* helped you figure out its meaning?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The words 'a sudden thunderstorm' helped because they give an example. Also, 'watched' tells me it is something you can see happen."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Keep using context clues today. When you find a word you don't know, look at the sentences around it before you skip it. Also, a *myth* is a traditional story that explains something about the world or a culture's beliefs."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Using context clues","tryThis":"Give a frame: 'The word ___ is near ___, which tells me it means ___.' Point to a single nearby clue word and have students underline it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Using context clues","tryThis":"Ask: Write your own sentence that uses *phenomenon* so that a classmate could figure out its meaning from context alone."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students read aloud with attention to pausing and meaning, then extract facts from assigned paragraphs. Part B: Groups predict what myths from this world would explain, create prediction posters, and compare across texts and authors.","activities":[{"id":"lia-fluency-and-read","title":"Part A: Read, Pause, and Extract Facts","minutes":13,"standards":["RI.6.1","L.6.4.a","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Preparation: Before class, select one short paragraph (3-5 sentences) from each Newsela text. Choose paragraphs that mention daily life, beliefs about gods or nature, learning, or hardships such as farming, weather, or sea travel. Make enough copies for groups of 3-4. Assign each group one text: A Short History of Greek and Roman Myth, Ancient Greece: The First Greeks, or Ancient Greek Thinkers, Truth Seekers. Have at least one group per text if possible."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"A Short History of Greek and Roman Myth; Ancient Greece: The First Greeks; Ancient Greek Thinkers, Truth Seekers","pages":"One teacher-selected paragraph per group"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Good readers pause on purpose. A comma, a period, or a dash tells your voice when to slow down so the meaning comes through. Listen as I read two sentences from a paragraph. Notice where I pause and where my voice rises."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model reading the first two sentences of one selected paragraph aloud, with deliberate pauses at commas and periods and slight emphasis on the most important idea. Then ask the metacognitive questions below."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why did I pause here? What idea did I emphasize?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"You paused after 'the Greeks believed' because the next part tells what they believed. You stressed the word 'gods' because that is the main idea about their beliefs."},{"type":"directions","text":"In your group, take turns reading your paragraph aloud, one sentence at a time. Read for accuracy first, then pause where the punctuation tells you to. After each reader, the group asks: Why did the author pause here? What idea is emphasized? Then annotate: underline 3-4 facts about Greek life, beliefs, learning, or daily challenges and circle any unfamiliar words. Use context clues to guess the meaning of each circled word."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and listen for accuracy and phrasing. If a student reads word by word with no pauses, model one sentence and have them echo it. Praise students who explain a pause using the meaning of the sentence, not just the punctuation."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["L.6.4.a"],"stem":"A student reads this sentence from an assigned paragraph: 'Farmers feared drought, a long period with no rain, because their crops would die.' What does the word *drought* most likely mean?","choices":[{"text":"A long period without rain","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The phrase right after the word, 'a long period with no rain,' defines it, and the crops dying confirms the meaning."},{"text":"A kind of crop farmers grow","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. Crops are mentioned, but the sentence says crops die because of the drought, so it cannot be a crop."},{"text":"A god that farmers worshipped","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The sentence doesn't mention a god, and the words after the comma explain the word as a condition, not a being."},{"type":"x","text":"","correct":false,"rationale":""}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading aloud with clear phrasing and in using verbs precisely to report facts from the text (ELD.PI.6.6, ELD.PII.6.3).","sayAsk":"Say: 'Let's report what the text says.' Offer frames: 'The text states that ___.' 'The author explains that ___.' 'Greeks believed ___.' For Emerging students, use simple present and past verbs: 'Farmers needed rain.' For Expanding and Bridging, add reporting verbs (states, describes, suggests) and perfect forms: 'The author has shown that ___.' Let students rehearse one sentence aloud with a partner before reading to the group.","watchFor":"If a student reads accurately but without pausing, then model a sentence and invite choral echo reading. If a student names a fact without citing the text, then prompt: 'Which words told you that?' Success: students read a sentence with appropriate pauses and report a fact using a reporting verb."}]},{"id":"lia-predict-posters","title":"Part B: Prediction Posters and Comparing Across Texts","minutes":17,"standards":["RI.6.1","RI.6.7","RI.6.9","L.6.4.a","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Gallery Walk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With your group, create a prediction poster with two parts. Left side: 3-4 facts from your paragraph, each with a quote or the words that show it. Right side: Predict how stories from a world like this might sound. What fears, natural events, or mysteries would people try to explain? Write at least two predictions, each beginning with 'Because the text says ___, stories might explain ___.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Your evidence goes on the left, and your thinking goes on the right. Each prediction has to connect to a fact. That is how we use text evidence to support an inference."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one fact from your text, and what kind of story might come from it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text says Greek sailors faced sudden storms on the sea. Stories might explain storms by saying an angry sea god causes them."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Because students have only words, remind them that they are building a mental picture from the text. Encourage them to include a sentence on their poster that describes what they imagine, such as 'I picture ___ because the text says ___.' This connects to RI.6.7: understanding a topic through words alone, which students will later compare with visual media."},{"type":"directions","text":"Gallery walk: Post your poster. Visit two posters from groups that read a different text. Use sticky notes to write one similarity and one difference between their predictions and yours. Then return to your poster and read the notes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How are the predictions across different texts alike or different? Why might each author's text lead to a different focus?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Our text was about the first Greeks, so we predicted stories about farming and weather. The group with the thinkers text predicted stories about big questions, like why people exist. The author of the myth history text focused on how stories changed over time, but the other authors focused on how people lived and thought."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When two authors write about the same world, they choose different details to show. One author might emphasize daily hardships, and another might emphasize ideas and learning. Comparing them gives us a fuller picture of ancient Greece than any one text alone."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students share predictions and compare ideas across groups using conditional and modal language and respectful turn-taking (ELD.PI.6.1, ELD.PII.6.3).","sayAsk":"Offer frames: 'I predict that stories might explain ___ because ___.' 'Our text states ___, but your text describes ___.' 'I agree with ___, and I would add ___.' For Emerging students, allow pointing to a fact on the poster and using: 'Greeks needed ___. Stories explain ___.' Expanding and Bridging students should paraphrase a partner's idea before adding their own.","watchFor":"If a student states a prediction with no evidence, then prompt: 'Which fact supports that?' If a student only agrees, then prompt: 'What would you add?' Success: students link a fact to a prediction using because and might, and respond to another group's idea."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Connecting a fact to a prediction","tryThis":"Provide a two-column organizer, 'The text says' and 'A story might explain,' and complete the first row together using a sentence from the paragraph."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Comparing authors' presentations","tryThis":"Ask: Which author's paragraph made Greek life feel the most challenging, and which words created that feeling? Write two sentences that cite wording from each text."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize facts and predictions about ancient Greece and connect them to the purpose of myths.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: Worlds Shape Stories","minutes":5,"standards":["RI.6.1","RI.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use the Quick Write routine to respond. Include at least one fact from a text and one new idea you learned from another group's poster."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How might the real challenges and beliefs of ancient Greek life lead people to create myths?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text says Greeks depended on farming and the sea, so storms and droughts were scary. Stories about gods who control weather could explain those things and make people feel less helpless. Another group's text said Greek thinkers asked big questions, so myths may also explain mysteries about life."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the Quick Writes as a formative check. Look for evidence tied to a prediction and for use of context clues or the word phenomenon. Use what you find to plan for Lesson 3."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional independent reading and reflection.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Independent Reading and Fluency Practice","minutes":0,"standards":["RI.6.1"],"routine":"Independent Reading","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read your independent reading book for 20 minutes. Then choose one paragraph and read it aloud twice, pausing to show the meaning. In your reading log, write one sentence about why the author paused and what idea was emphasized."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students read teacher-selected paragraphs from three Newsela informational texts about ancient Greece, extract facts, and predict what fears, natural events, and mysteries Greek myths would explain. They create prediction posters, compare predictions and authors' presentations across texts, and practice prosody with metacognitive questions about pauses.","keyActivities":["Launch Turn and Talk with context-clue modeling for phenomenon","Fluency modeling and group oral reading with 'Why did the author pause?' questions","Fact extraction and annotation from assigned Newsela paragraphs","Prediction posters and gallery walk comparing across texts","Quick Write linking Greek life to the creation of myths"],"vocabularyTaught":["context clue","phenomenon","myth","prediction","prosody"],"standardsCovered":["L.6.4.a","RI.6.1","RI.6.7","RI.6.9","SL.6.1","ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PII.6.3"]}}
